healthInfo.healthcareSystem: Universal (National Health Insurance / 국민건강보험 — mandatory for residents)
healthInfo.qualityNotes: Excellent healthcare system with world-class hospitals and advanced technology. English is available at larger hospitals in Seoul and Busan but limited elsewhere. Healthcare is affordable by Western standards. National Health Insurance does NOT cover tourists — you pay out-of-pocket or through travel insurance.
healthInfo.pharmacyHours: Most pharmacies (약국) open 9am-9pm. Some are open 24/7 in larger cities. Look for the green '약' sign. Some medications are available only at hospitals, not regular pharmacies.
healthInfo.pharmacyTips: Pharmacies are widely available. Many medications require a prescription. Some common medications are available OTC. Prescription medications must be dispensed at a pharmacy with a valid Korean prescription. Hospital prescriptions can be filled at external pharmacies.
healthInfo.prescriptionRules: Most medications require a Korean doctor's prescription. Foreign prescriptions are NOT accepted. You must see a Korean doctor to get a prescription. Some controlled substances require special permits.

restrictedMeds.name: Pseudoephedrine (Sudafed and similar)
restrictedMeds.note: Medications containing pseudoephedrine are prohibited. Sudafed, Contac, and similar products cannot be brought into South Korea.

restrictedMeds.name: Adderall/amphetamines (ADHD medications)
restrictedMeds.note: Strictly prohibited. ADHD medications containing amphetamines or methylphenidate (Adderall, Ritalin, Vyvanse, Concerta) are illegal to bring into South Korea.

restrictedMeds.name: Codeine-containing medications
restrictedMeds.note: Codeine is controlled. A prescription is required.

restrictedMeds.name: Medical cannabis
restrictedMeds.note: Cannabis is illegal in South Korea with severe penalties.

healthInfo.bringDocumentation: Carry a doctor's letter listing all medications with generic names. Bring sufficient supply in original packaging. For any potentially problematic medications, contact the Korean embassy before travel. Controlled medications require a permit from KDF (Korea Drug & Food International).

travelInsurance.requiredNote: Not legally required but essential — healthcare costs can add up quickly without coverage.
travelInsurance.tips: National Health Insurance does not cover tourists. Large hospitals often require payment upfront or guarantee of payment from your insurance. International clinics are popular with tourists. Keep all receipts for insurance reimbursement.

healthInfo.waterNotes: Tap water is safe to drink in South Korea. Bottled water is also widely available.
healthInfo.foodSafetyTips: Korean cuisine is generally very safe. Bibimbap, kimchi, bulgogi, and most Korean dishes are safe from restaurants. Raw fish (회) is popular — ensure it's from a reputable restaurant. Be cautious with very spicy food if you're not used to it. Food from street vendors (pojangmacha) is generally safe.
sources: South Korea Ministry of Food and Drug Safety
healthInfo.medicalTourismNote: South Korea is a major medical tourism destination, particularly for cosmetic surgery, dermatology, and advanced medical treatments. High quality at moderate costs.

healthcare.costForTourists: South Korea is a medical tourism powerhouse. Even without insurance, costs are reasonable. Clinic visit $30-60. ER $100-300. World-class hospitals at 30-50% of US prices.
healthcare.pharmacyAccess: Pharmacies (약국, yakguk) common. Some medications that are prescription-only in the US are OTC in Korea. Pharmacists may not speak English — use Google Translate.
healthcare.hospitalNotes: Samsung Medical Center, Asan Medical Center, Severance Hospital are world-class. International clinics in Itaewon/Gangnam cater to foreigners with English-speaking staff. Healthcare quality is excellent throughout the country.
healthcare.insuranceAdvice: Travel insurance recommended but healthcare is affordable even out-of-pocket.

controlledSubstances.note: Classified as 'psychotropic substances.' Extremely strict — even with a valid foreign prescription, you can be arrested.
All cannabis products are illegal. Korean law applies even to consumption abroad — Korean nationals can be prosecuted for cannabis use in countries where it's legal.
Available only at pharmacies with ID registration.

medications.generalAdvice: South Korea has extremely strict drug laws. Bring a doctor's letter and original prescriptions for ALL medications. When in doubt, contact the Korean embassy before travel.

scams.name: Overpriced soju tent (pojangmacha) bills
scams.description: Tourist-area tents charge 3-5x normal prices. A few soju bottles and snacks become a $100+ bill.
scams.avoidance: Check prices before ordering. Real pojangmacha prices: soju ~3,000-5,000 KRW, snacks ~10,000-20,000 KRW. Go to non-tourist areas.

scams.name: Taxi refusal and overcharging
scams.description: Some taxi drivers refuse to use meters for foreigners or take long routes. Late at night, some demand flat rates.
scams.avoidance: Use KakaoTaxi app (Korea's Uber). Insist on the meter. Orange international taxis have English-speaking drivers.

connectivity.simOptions: KT, SKT, or LG U+ SIM/eSIM at airports. $15-30 for 5-30 days with unlimited data. Korea has the world's fastest mobile internet. eSIM via Airalo.
connectivity.wifiAvailability: Free WiFi literally everywhere — subway, buses, public spaces, cafes. Korea has the best public WiFi infrastructure in the world.
connectivity.bestOption: WiFi alone might be sufficient in Seoul. For travel outside Seoul, grab a KT SIM/eSIM at the airport.

cultural.tipping: Not expected and can be seen as rude in traditional settings. No tipping at restaurants, taxis, or hotels. International hotels may accept tips.
cultural.dressCode: Smart casual. Koreans are fashion-conscious. Cover up at temples. Modest dress is appreciated.
cultural.greetings: Bow — deeper for elders. Handshake with both hands for respect. Use two hands when giving/receiving objects. 'Annyeonghaseyo' for hello.
taboos: Writing someone's name in red ink (associated with death)
Blowing your nose at the table
Sticking chopsticks upright in rice (funeral ritual)
Pouring your own drink (someone else should pour for you)
Refusing a drink from an elder (at least accept and sip)
cultural.haggling: Only at traditional markets (Namdaemun, Dongdaemun). Not at restaurants, department stores, or convenience stores.

safety.lgbtSafety: No anti-discrimination law. Socially conservative but safe. Seoul has LGBTQ+ scene in Itaewon/Jongno.
safety.soloFemaleSafety: Very safe. South Korea has low crime rates. Well-lit cities, excellent public transit. Some drunk men can be pushy late at night.
safety.notes: South Korea is one of the safest countries in the world. Violent crime is extremely rare. Main concern is the omnipresent hidden camera issue (molka) in some public restrooms.

practical.visaFreeCountries: US citizens: K-ETA required ($10), 90 days. UK: 90 days visa-free. Most EU: 90 days.
practical.bestTimeToVisit: April-May (spring, cherry blossoms) and September-November (autumn foliage). Summer is hot and humid. Winter is cold.
